# Data Minimisation

GDPR Art. 5(1)(c): personal data must be *adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary* for
the purpose. It is the principle that makes every other privacy obligation cheaper — data never
collected needs no legal basis, no retention schedule, no breach notification and no deletion
mechanism.

[[privacy-policy-template]] names it and then organises §4 around it:

> "We practise **data minimisation** — we collect as little as possible."
> — privacy-policy/PRIVACY_POLICY.md, 2026-07-10

## What survives the principle

| Category | What it is | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Information you provide | email address and message content, only if you choose to write | directly from you |
| Technical / log data | standard server logs from the host — IP, user-agent, pages requested, timestamp | automatically, via the hosting provider |
| Cookies | **none set by this Service by default** | — |

Two categories, one of which the site does not choose to collect and cannot switch off — it is a
by-product of being hosted at all, which is why it lands on [[controller-vs-processor]] rather than
on the controller's own conscience. Sensitive categories (government IDs, health, biometric,
precise geolocation, racial or ethnic origin, religion, financial account data) are excluded
explicitly, with a request not to send them.

## Why the discipline compounds

Because collection is near-zero, most of the policy's remaining sections can make **absolute**
rather than hedged statements: no analytics, no advertising, no fingerprinting, no profiling, no
automated decision-making with legal effect, no sale or sharing, no "Do Not Sell" mechanism
required. Each of those is a claim the document can only make because §4 is short.

The same relationship works in reverse, and is the standing risk on
[[one-reusable-policy-not-per-project]]: apply this template to a project that *does* collect —
accounts, a database, a third-party API — and the absolute statements downstream become false
without anyone editing them.

## The interaction with legal bases

Minimisation and [[gdpr-legal-bases]] are not independent. The policy leans on **legitimate
interests** for operating and securing the Service, which is the basis with a balancing test
attached; a minimal dataset is what makes that test easy to pass. Consent is reserved for the one
thing the visitor initiates — email — where it is unambiguous.
